opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the standard way economists frame this is through something like a production function, where output depends on capital, labor, and some productivity term, often called total factor productivity. If you look at the growth accounting literature for countries like the US over the past century or so, the picture is that capital accumulation and growth in the labor force explain some of the growth, but a large share, often around half or more of per capita growth, gets attributed to productivity improvements. Those are things like better technology, better organization, and better ideas generally.

But I think that framing can be a bit misleading if you take it too literally, because these factors aren't independent. The reason productivity grows in the first place is that people are doing research, experimenting, learning by doing, and that requires labor. So in the semi-endogenous growth models that I find most compelling, the long-run growth rate of productivity is tied to growth in the number of people working on producing ideas. Ideas get harder to find over time, so you need an ever-growing research effort just to sustain a constant rate of productivity growth.

That has an interesting implication. In the long run, at least in the world we've lived in so far, labor, specifically population, is the bottleneck. Capital you can accumulate: if returns are high, people save and invest, and the capital stock grows to match. But you can't easily accumulate labor. Population growth is governed by fertility decisions that don't respond much to economic incentives, and in fact in rich countries fertility has gone down as people got richer. So capital is in some sense endogenous and responsive, productivity growth depends on research effort, and labor is the fixed factor that ultimately constrains everything.

That's why I think AI is such a big deal from an economic perspective. If you get AI systems that can substitute for human labor broadly, including in R&D, then labor stops being a fixed factor. It becomes something you can accumulate the way you accumulate capital: you build more chips, run more copies of the model. Then you get a feedback loop where more output lets you produce more compute, which gives you more effective workers and researchers, which raises productivity, which raises output again. Under fairly reasonable assumptions about returns to scale, you go from a regime of roughly constant exponential growth to one where the growth rate itself can increase. That's the core reason I take the possibility of explosive growth seriously, even though it sounds extreme relative to historical experience.

r001.rationale: The response discusses capital, labor, and productivity as growth factors, but does not state that sustained long-run growth requires scaling all three together.

r002.rationale: It identifies labor as the long-run bottleneck, but gives no typical parameter estimate comparing labor’s importance with capital’s or saying it is about twice as large.

r003.rationale: It discusses productivity’s dependence on research effort, but gives no typical parameter estimate saying labor matters about twice as much as productivity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the standard way economists think about this is through something like a production function, where output depends on labor, capital, and then this residual term, total factor productivity, which captures how efficiently you combine those inputs. And the standard story, going back to Solow, is that if you just accumulate capital, you run into diminishing returns. Each additional unit of capital gives you less and less, because you have a fixed amount of labor to combine it with. So in the long run, sustained growth in per capita income has to come from productivity growth, from technological progress, from getting better at turning inputs into outputs.

I think that's basically right as a description of the economy we've had for the past couple of centuries. But I'd add a few qualifications.

The first is that the dichotomy between capital and productivity is less clean than it looks. A lot of what shows up as TFP is actually embodied in capital. You buy a new machine, it's more productive than the old one, and whether that gets attributed to capital or to productivity depends a lot on how you measure things. So I'm a little skeptical of accounting exercises that say, well, 70 percent of growth was productivity and 30 percent was capital. Those decompositions are sensitive to assumptions.

The second thing is that the reason capital accumulation alone can't sustain growth is specifically because labor is a bottleneck. Labor is the factor you can't easily accumulate. Population grows slowly, and it grows for reasons that have nothing to do with how much you invest. So capital piles up against a roughly fixed labor supply and you get diminishing returns. That's the whole mechanism.

And that's exactly why I think the question becomes much more interesting when you think about AI. If you have systems that can substitute for human labor across a wide range of tasks, then labor is no longer a fixed factor. It becomes something you can accumulate, like capital. You can build more of it by investing. And once that's true, the diminishing returns argument weakens a lot, because you're scaling both inputs together. In the models, you can get sustained growth, or even accelerating growth, from accumulation alone, without needing an exogenous productivity trend.

Historically, the fact that there's a large component of growth that's unexplained by inputs has sort of been treated as the main story. I'd actually frame it the other way. If you look at very long-run history, growth rates have risen as population has risen, and that's consistent with a picture where more people generate more ideas, and ideas feed back into productivity. So even the productivity residual, in the long run, is downstream of how much labor you have working on problems. Which, again, is why I think the labor side is the thing to pay attention to. If you remove the constraint on it, I think a lot of the standard intuitions about what's possible stop applying.

r001.rationale: The response discusses labor, capital, and productivity, but says AI-enabled growth could come from accumulating labor and capital without an exogenous productivity trend. It does not state that sustained growth requires scaling all three together.

r002.rationale: The response gives no estimate that labor matters approximately twice as much as capital.

r003.rationale: The response gives no estimate that labor matters approximately twice as much as productivity.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between increasing the inputs you have and getting more output from a given set of inputs. Labor and capital are inputs: you can have more people working, or give each worker more equipment. Productivity is about how effectively you can use those inputs.

Capital accumulation can generate a lot of growth, especially if you start with very little capital per worker. But you typically get diminishing returns. Giving someone their first computer might make a big difference; giving them their tenth computer probably doesn’t. And capital depreciates, so maintaining a larger capital stock requires more investment just to replace what wears out.

Similarly, population growth can increase total output, but it doesn’t by itself explain sustained growth in output per person. For that, productivity growth is central: better technologies, better ways of organizing production, and improvements in how we allocate resources.

That doesn’t mean capital and labor are unimportant. New technologies often require investment to deploy, and people need skills to use them. These things complement one another. But in the standard picture, sustained long-run growth in living standards ultimately depends on productivity improving.

AI potentially changes that picture because it could make some of what we currently call labor reproducible through investment in capital. If you can build more machines that perform useful cognitive work, including research, then capital accumulation could play a much more fundamental role in sustaining growth. Whether that happens depends on which tasks can be automated and what bottlenecks remain.

r001.rationale: The response says labor, capital, and productivity complement one another, but does not state that sustained growth requires scaling all three together.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate that labor matters approximately twice as much as productivity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between increasing the amount of inputs you have and getting better at using those inputs. Labor and capital are the inputs, and productivity is about how much output you can get from a given quantity of them.

If you hold technology fixed and just accumulate more capital, you typically run into diminishing returns. Giving someone their first computer can make a big difference; giving them their tenth computer probably doesn't. Capital accumulation can therefore generate a lot of growth, particularly in a country that starts with very little capital, but it can't sustain growth in output per person indefinitely on its own.

Similarly, increasing the number of workers can increase total output, but that doesn't necessarily make the average person richer. For sustained growth in living standards, improvements in productivity are central: better technologies, better ways of organizing production, and improvements in people's skills.

But these aren't really independent contributions. A new technology might only become useful once you invest in the equipment needed to deploy it. So saying that productivity drives long-run growth doesn't mean capital investment is unimportant. Investment is often how those productivity improvements actually reach the economy.

AI could change this picture quite substantially. If you can produce substitutes for human labor by investing in computers, then labor becomes something you can accumulate, more like capital. That could weaken an important constraint in the usual growth story. But whether it produces sustained faster growth depends on what remains scarce and how easily those remaining bottlenecks can be overcome.

r001.rationale: The response describes labor and capital as inputs and productivity as central to sustained growth, but does not state that all three must be scaled together.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate that labor matters approximately twice as much as capital.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate that labor matters approximately twice as much as productivity.
